This person claimed that if his most noted endeavor was not successful, he would "throw the whole of what I have attempted over the bridge." This former employee of Jedediah Strutt and Richard Arkwright entered into a partnership with William Almy and Moses Brown. This person's scheme of management was modeled on British villages, depended on woman and child workers, and was dubbed the "Rhode Island system" for his state of residence. This person ushered in a period of industrialization that peaked with the Waltham-Lowell system. Name this "Father of the American Industrial Revolution" who smuggled British textile technology to the U.S. In his brain.

One prince of this kingdom was a shepherd who either died of a snake-bite in the heel or was killed by the Nemean Lion. Shortly before her death, Alcmene undertook a journey from this place to Thebes, but died en route at Megara. This place was ruled by a king who prevailed in a womb quarrel with his brother, to whom he gave rule of Tiryns. This place enjoyed a prosperous five year reign under a man who broke Aeneas's hip by throwing a stone and won the chariot race at Patroclus's funeral games. This kingdom was jointly ruled by Proetus and a man who was killed by a discus by Perseus years after locking up Danae in a bronze tower. Ruled by Acrisius, its throne went to Diomedes directly from his grandfather, the organizer of the Seven Against Thebes. Name this Peloponnesian kingdom whose inhabitants gave their name to the Greek side during the Trojan War.

One member of this dynasty, with a name meaning "Hawk," tried to form a splinter state during the rule of his brother, a ruler from this dynasty known as "Callinicus." Near the end of the life of this dynasty's founder, he crushed Lysimachus of Thrace at Corupedium. The rulers of this dynasty agreed to the Peace of Apamea with Rome after Eudamos defeated this dynasty's army, which was commanded by an exiled Carthaginian. This dynasty's founder, who was slain by a man sent by Ptolemy, defeated Demetrius the Besieger and Antigonus the One- Eyed at the 301 BCE Battle of Ipsus. This dynasty warred with Rome at the Eurymedon River under its ruler Antiochus the Great. Name this dynasty that ruled Syria and Mesopotamia in the wake of Alexander the Great's death, started by a general known as "Nicator."

AND BONUS In "Childe Harold's Pilgrimage," Byron compares Rome to this figure "of nations," while, in one speech, Hamlet compares his mother's tears to those of this figure. In one story, she provoked the jealousy of her sister-in-law Aedon, who accidentally killed her own son Itylus and was subsequently turned into a nightingale, while she was also sometimes associated with Phoroneus, either as his mother, daughter, or consort. The husband of Amphion, she was the daughter of a Phyrigian king and ruled over the city of Tantalus, and, after her most notable incident, she was turned into a stone formation in Mt. Sipylon. Her children, including Ismenos, Alphenor, and Ilioneus, were all killed by Apollo and Artemis after she cut short a festival honoring Leto. Name this woman from Greek myth who boasted of her seven sons and seven daughters.

This nation was briefly made independent after the efforts of Jose Nunez de Caceres, but it was invaded by a neighbor after only nine weeks. Its 1844 constitution was promulgated by a group known as the Trinitarians; they were led by Juan Pablo Duarte, Ramon Mella, and Francisco Sanchez. During the 1860s, the War of the Restoration was fought over Spanish influence here, but it ended up independent once more, this time under the auspices of Buenaventura Baez. Baez was himself succeeded by Ulises Heureaux, who plunged this nation into debt while bolstering the sugar industry. In 1916, it was invaded by U.S. Marines, who were nominally in control until their removal by Warren Harding. In 1930, this nation was taken over by a dictator who instigated the Parsley Massacre. Rafael Trujillo ruled over which Caribbean country with capital at Santo Domingo?

This man defeated an urpising led by Marduk-zakir-shummi II and his elamite allies at the Battle of Cutha. According to Herodotus, his army was defeated by Sethos at Pelusium after a plague of mice devoured their bowstrings. Another of his campaigns saw the sack of Lachish and the reinstatement of Padi; that effort had followed his forced deposition of Sidqia after the conquest of Joppa and Azjuru. His most notable campaign ended in the reception of tribute from Hezekiah, though that war fought against Judah notably did not feature a sack of Jerusalem. Succeeded by Esarhaddon after his assassination, this ruler moved his capital from Dur-Sharukkin, which his father Sargon II had established, back to Nineveh. Name this Assyrian king whose "cohorts were gleaming in purple and gold" in a poem about his destruction by Byron.

This man's death came at the hands of Yussuf Kothual, who managed to stab him in a desperate final attempt because this man, a legendary archer, lost his footing as he was about to kill Yussuf. That demise came as he was about to cross the Oxus River to conquer Turkestan. He came to power after the death of his uncle Togrul, which started a bitter war of succession with another of his uncles, Kutalmish. Much of his domestic policy and the consolidation of his empire was carried out by his advisor, Nizam-ul-Mulk. His campaigns against the Byzantine Empire started with his sack of Caesarea Mazaca but were initially met with defeat in Cilicia. He emerged victorious, however, in a battle the following year, mostly due to the defection of Cuman mercenaries. Name this Seljuk ruler who defeated Romanos IV Diogenes at the Battle of Manzikert.

The lead up to this conflict saw the signing of a "Corn Treaty" and the declaration of a state of invasion by a force known as the "British Band" by John Reynolds. Two battles during this conflict were fought at Apple River Fort and Waddams Grove, while two massacres were perpetrated at Spafford Farm and St. Vrain. Twelve men under John Giles Adams were killed, prompting a retreat to Dixon's Ferry, in this war's opening skirmish at Stillman's Run, while its decisive final battle, fought near Prairie du Chien, saw action by a ship called the Warrior that ignored surrender requests by White Cloud; that engagement was the Battle of Bad Axe. Its namesake, a rival of Keokuk, led a confederation of Sauk and Fox Indians across the Mississippi River. Name this war fought during the early 1830s.

This man negotiated the purchase of Polaris missiles via the Nassau Agreement after the U.S. Backed out of the development of the Skybolt system. One of his first actions was to try and boost employment as part of his One Nation philosophy, which led to the resignantion of three treasury ministers. One incident during his tenure as prime minister was the nuclear Windscale Accident. He had introduced premium bonds while serving as Chancellor of the Exchequer under his predecessor, Anthony Eden. He said that "This growth of national consciousness is a political fact" in his "Wind of Change" speech, delivered to the South African parliament, which echoed his granting of independence to many African colonies. He resigned after it was discovered that his Secretary of State for War was having an affair with Christine Keeler in the Profumo Affair. Name this conservative British prime minister.

One ruler of this polity ordered the construction of the Bayon Temple, which was famous for its fifty towers. That man came to power by driving the Champa Kingdom from this polity's former capital, though his son would later make concessions to Champa as well as give up the territory that would be used to found the Sukhothai Kingdom. This polity's next ruler would pay tribute to Kublai Khan to preserve his rule as well as oversee the destruction of many Buddhist statues in favor of his Hinduism. That ruler was deposed by his son-in-law, who received the Chinese diplomat Chou Ta-kuan and was named Srindravarman. Several rulers named Jayavarman and Suryavarman also ruled this kingdom known for constructing the temple complex of Angkor Wat. Name this empire based in Cambodia.

This king's unpopular adviser Michael de la Pole was ousted with the help of the so-called Wonderful Parliament. Forces loyal to this king, led by Robert de Vere, were defeated at Radcot Bridge by a group that purged his court in the Merciless Parliament. Ten years later, he arrested and tried that group, which included the Duke of Gloucester and the Earl of Warwick, the Lords Appellant. His marriage to Anne of Bohemia failed to result in the strong military alliance he had hoped for, and he moved the capital to Chelmsford for five days to escape violence fermented by John Ball and Wat Tyler, who led the Peasent's Revolt during his reign. His reign was finally ended by a son of John of Gaunt named Henry of Bollingbroke, whom he unsuccessfully tried to disinherit. Name this Plantagenet son of Edward the Black Prince, the predecessor of Henry IV.

They were handed out to those who took part in the so-called "Prussian voyages" as well as to those who fought the Cathars in South-western France. As an incentive, they were given out to participants in any approved passagium generale, and they were a natural extension of taking up the cross. They were first granted en-masse during the Council of Clermont for those soldiers who set out to the Levant. The morality of their granting declined after the Crusades, and "As soon as a coin in the coffer rings / the soul from purgatory springs" was claimed by a Dominican named Johann Tetzel, who was selling these when he entered Wittenberg, heavily upsetting Martin Luther. Name this Church practice of forgiving sins after atonement which were often sold before the Reformation.

He fought a battle of where he was able to deploy his troops from the march and turn away an attack on his flank by Gibamund. After killing Ammatas, the brother of King Gelimer, he was able to rout the enemy at Ad Decimum, and he killed another brother of Gelimer, Tzazon, in a victory shortly thereafter. His bucellari cavalry units won him a victory at Dara over the Sassanids, and would later deceive Witigies by a ruse and take Ravenna. He lost at Callinicum, forcing his nation to sign an "Endless Peace." His forces entered the Hippodrome and helped put down the Nika revolt, but upon his replacement by his rival Narses, a court eunuch, legend has it that he was blinded and forced to beg in Rome. Name this general who reconquered large parts of the former Western Roman Empire for the Byzantine Emperor Justinian I.

He commanded the Army of the Vosges for the Third French Republic during the Franco-Prussian War, and earlier, during the War of the Tatters, he had supported Brazilian Gauchos. He sacked Gualeguaychu while supporting the Colorados against the Blancos, who were backed by Manuel Oribe and Juan Manuel de Rosas, in the Uruguayan Civil War. In a different country, he organized a unit called the "Hunters of the Alps," but was disappointed when his hometown of Nice was handed to the French. He proceeded to win victories at Calatafimi and Volturno as the leader of the Expedition of a Thousand, after which he gave over his conquests to the new nation of Italy despite his contempt for Cavour. Name figure from the Italian Risorgimento movement, the leader of the Redshirts.

At the time of his death, he was planning to write a review of the seven sciences from a moralistic point of view, but he only completed the volume on mathematics. This author of The Subjective Synthesis distinguished between the spiritual and the temporal in his work "Considerations of the Spritual Power," and his other early essays include "A General Distinction Between Opinions and Desires." The coiner of the term "altruism," he developed a tripartite law which stated that civilization was to go from animism to polytheism to monotheism during its theological stage before moving onto the pseudo-scientific metaphysical stage and then finally reaching the final stage, where all is based on science and empirical observation. Name this French founder of positivism.

The aggressors in this conflict decided on a three-pronged plan of attack; their left flank, under the command of Evelyn Wood, decided not to engage the enemy after camping at Tinta's Kraal. Their right flank, which was led by Charles Pearson, fought a small battle near the Inyezane River and was besieged at Eshowe after they crossed the Tugela River. The central units, commanded by Lord Chelmsford, failed to establish a defensive position and were decisively defeated, after which a smaller contingent of troops scored a major victory at Rorke's Drift. Ended by the Battle of Ulundi, this conflict had earlier seen a British defeat at the Battle of Isandlwana. Name this war fought against a namesake African tribe led by Cetshwayo.

One person associated with this movement authored the essay "A Plea for the West" and was known for denying admission to African-American students at the educational institute he ran in Cincinnati. Another person associated with this movement served for fifteen years as president of Oberlin College and wrote a series of articles about the freemasons. In addition to Lyman Beecher and Charles Grandison Finney, this movement encompassed the ideology of Barton Stone, who was present at Cane Ridge, Kentucky, for this movement's largest camp meeting. Ideologically, this movement was associated with congregationalism. Name this religious revival that took place during the early 19th Century that followed a similarly named event from the previous century.

One leader of this country allowed his power to pass to Leon Arguello, but gave it to his uncle when Arguello proved too independent. That leader of this country was assassinated during a banquet by Rigoberto Perez, and had earlier overthrown President Sacasa to gain power over this country. In the 1990's, this country's rule passed from the FSLN to the opposition led by Violeta de Chamorro. This nation was led by Jose Santos Zelaya and Luis and Anastasio Somoza, who killed the guerrilla leader Augusto Sandino. An American mercenary named William Walker conquered this country as a filibuster, and ruled it briefly during the 1850s. Name this country, once ruled by Daniel Ortega, whose Sandinistas were funded in the Iran-Contra affair.

According to contemporary historians, the fields on which this battle took place became so fecundated by the carapaces of the fallen that they were able to produce a "magna copia" of yield for many years. The losing side's two commanders disagreed many times; they refused to camp on the same side of a major river, and one of them attacked the opposing army's camp while their leader was negotiating with the other commander because they both wished to claim credit for the victory. An early skirmish during this battle saw a picketing force under Marcus Scaurus captured and executed. Name this battle, the second of the Cimbri War, between Boiorix and Teutobod, and Maximus and Caepio, which gave way to the Marian reforms because it was such a striking defeat for the Romans.

This leader won the so-called Coupon Election, which was the first election to feature universal male suffrage in his home nation. This man's government was opposed by the Wee Frees under William Benn after he ousted his predecessor, and he resigned after threatening Turkey with war during the Chanak Crisis. Among the social reforms he promulgated was an Education Act written by Herbert Fischer that raised the age for leaving school to fourteen. Also the prime mover behind the Old Age Pensions Act, this leader advocated his People's Budget as Chancellor of the Exchequer under Lord Asquith, whom he replaced as Prime Minister. Name this Welshman, the prime minister who represented Britain at the Treaty of Versailles and served during the later parts of World War One.

This decision was modified by the "good faith exception" set down in US v. Leon. The decision for this case forced the states to apply a principle first set down in Weeks v. United States. Justice Harlan's dissent claimed that there was no reason to reconsider the case of Wolf v. Colorado, while the majority opinion for this case was written by Thomas Clark. Police had entered the defendant's house searching for a bomb suspect or evidence of illegal gambling, but, even though obscene materials were found, because the police could not produce a warrant, the exclusionary principle was applied. Name this Supreme Court case in which evidence was barred from trial because its confiscation violated the Fourth Amendment.

One of these pieces of legislation included sections restricting the employment of housekeepers, while a lesser known one of these changed the national flag to the main ruling party's and forbade the raising or display of the new national flag or colors by certain groups. An elaboration of several of the Twenty-Five Points released in 1920, this legislation included the Law for the Protection of Blood and Honor, while another one of these limited national citizenship to those who could prove bloodline purity and included the dismissal of a target group from the civil service, schools, and colleges. Name these pieces of legislation passed at the Nationalist Socialst party congress on September 15, 1935 in a namesake Bavarian city that promulgated many anti-semitic measures.

He codified the statutes at Oxford University and changed the focus of church services to the communion table from the pulpit in an attempt to limit Puritan sermons with the support of his vicar-general Nathaniel Brent. This man authorized raids on underground conventicles and he also created the etcetera oath that forced one to swear perptetual allegiance to the government of the bishops. This man's attempt to enforce the Book of Common Prayer in Scotland created the National Covenant movement that pledged to depose every new bishop, and he was imprisoned in the Tower of London for four years after being impeached by the Long Parliament. Decapitated for high treason in 1645, name this Archbishop of Canterbury who served from 1633 to 1645 and who held absolute power during the reign of Charles I.

Stanley Milgram wrote an article on "Nationality and" this phenomenon. In Escape from Freedom, Erich Fromm identified authoritarianism, destructiveness, and this as escape mechanisms. Herbert Kelman classified it into three major types, including identification and internalization, and when many individuals engage in this behavior, informational cascades result. Muzafer Sherif studied this phenomenon using a visual illusion in which a stationary light presented in a dark room appears to move, which is known as the autokinetic effect. Its occurence increases with group cohesiveness. It was most famously studied in an experiment framed as a vision test, where subjects were presented with lines labeled A, B, C and asked to judge their length in the presence of confederates. Identify this behavior studied by Solomon Asch.

General Juan Buendia defeated Luis Arteaga near Tarapaca in this conflict, and two countries' land armies were completely destroyed at the Battle of the Halt of Alliance during this war. The Lackawanna Conference, held on a U.S. Ship, attempted to end this conflict, but was ended by extortion raids by Patricio Lynch showing one side's complete dominance. The Cochrane and the Blanco Encalada were one side's main vessels, while the other side lost its main ship, the Huascar, after the Battle of Punta Angamos. The losing side ceded Antofagasta, Arica, and Tacna to its southern neighbor in the Treaty of Ancon at this conflict's close. Name this 1879 South American war that saw Chile defeat Peru and Bolivia along a namesake body of water.

This thinker gave a speech at the Freud Museum in London which was later published as Archive Fever. After publishing the essay "Signature Event Context," this philosopher became involved in a debate with John Searle over the speech acts theory of J.L. Austin. He developed the concept of hauntology and listed ten plagues of global capitalism in Specters of Marx, while another of this man's works undertakes both a "violent decipherment" of Genet and a separate discussion of Hegel in two adjacent columns. Well after writing Glas, this man discussed Husserl's theory of signs in Speech and Phenomena, and he wrote about Saussure, Rousseau, and Levi-Strauss in a book translated to English by Gayatri Spivak. He coined the title term for deferral of meaning in the essay "Differánce." identify this philosopher who introduced deconstruction in Of Grammatology.

While acting as the Count of Mortain, he married his first wife Isabel, but later annulled the marriage after discovering that they shared the same great-grandfather. He became monarch without a wife, but his marriage to Isabella of Angouleme triggered a war with France. In that war, Arthur of Brittany, who held some claim to this man's throne, was captured, and Anjou and Maine were retaken by Philip II. Following this king's failure in France, Pope Innocent III excommunicated him for refusing to accept Stephen Langton as the new Archbishop of Canterbury. Langton supported barons who launched a rebellion in the early 13th century that led to reforms in this man's monarchy. Name this King of England that lost Normandy to the French and signed the Magna Carta.

A recent decision from a panel created by this treaty found that "zeroing" violated U.S. Law, so the Department of Commerce would not be allowed to consider average prices over actual prices from exporters. The panel on Article 1904 of this document only made one decision that didn't involve the U.S. – an antidumping conclusion based on rolled steel – while a notable 2005 decision about this document was on the issue of softwood lumber. Brian Mulroney was re-elected in 1988 while defending a proposal for this document agreed upon with George Bush, though ultimately Jean Chretien and Clinton signed it with Carlos Salinas. Drafted shortly after the Maastricht Treaty that created the European Union, name this agreement that set up a trade bloc between the U.S., Canada, and Mexico.

This object is seen thumbing its nose at a German U-boat sailor in Mr. Punch's History of the Great War, in response to the US entering WWI, with the object saying it is "über alles" in its namesake "repartee". In the late 18th century, Marie Antoinette was given flowers associated with this object as part of a publicity campaign by Parmentier, who also kept this crop guarded by soldiers who were told to accept bribes, so that it would appear valuable and peasants could steal them. It was grown in the Tuilieres Garden during the Paris Commune to stave off starvation, and it was planted to feed families after the shrinkage of farm plots in Ireland. Introduced to Europe from the new world, name this starchy vegetable whose famine in the 1840s led to a massive emigration to North America.

This leader defeated the Anakims and conquered Goshen, and, after battling a coalition led by Jabin, he burned the city of Hazor to the ground. He enabled the conquest of Ai by extracting a confession from Achan and then leading Achan to the valley of Achor to be stoned to death. On Gibeon, he commanded the sun and moon to stand still, and he conquered one city by conducting parades around its walls for a week until they fell apart. The son of Nun, this student of Eleazar had one of his achievements honoured at Gilgal with a monument of twelve stones, and he led Ephraim himself after he divided Canaan between the twelve tribes of Israel. Name this judge who conquered Jericho and led the Israelites across the Jordan River, a friend of Caleb and the successor of Moses.

When this man shared some dangerous plans with William Claus, they got leaked to the U.S. Government via James Henry Craig. He defeated William Dudley's relief troops while he was laying siege to Fort Meigs, and his troops got attacked while he was occupied in talks at Vincennes, forcing him to flee to Moraviantown, near Chatham, Ontario. Supposedly killed by future Vice- President Richard M. Johnson, it was this leader's troops, supplemented by British forces under Isaac Brock, that scared away William Hull, leading to the 1812 capture of Detroit. Killed in the Battle of the Thames, this man is best known for travelling around America building a Native American Confederacy. Name this Shawnee leader and an enemy of William Henry Harrison, the brother of the Prophet Tenskwatawa.

This leader was asked, "How long will you allow the state to [remain] without a head?" when, according to Tacitus, his faux-humility almost led him to accidentally decline the job of emperor. Prior to becoming emperor, he won a triumph for quelling a rebellion in Pannonia. He distanced himself from the murder trial of his friend Calpurnius Piso, the governor of Syria, which led to the death of his adoptive son Germanicus. Pressured into divorcing Vipsania and marrying Julia the Elder, this emperor exiled himself to Rhodes as a young man and exiled himself to the island of Capri as a sitting emperor; he required the assistance of Macro in deposing of the man who assumed power during his virtual retirement, Sejanus. Name this Second Emperor of Rome, who ruled between Augustus and Caligula.

This monarch's reign saw the Statute of Provisors and the Statute of Praemunire passed in resistance to the papacy, and this monarch led a failed expedition in the Lothians a decade after defeating David II at the Battle of Neville's Cross. Guilty of installing Edward Baliol as a puppet king of Scotland shortly after signing the Treaty of Northampton, he saw his mistress Alice Perrers prosecuted by the Good Parliament. Reigning effectively from the time he got Roger Mortimer sentenced to death, this husband of Philippa of Hainault gained possession of Aquitaine but gave up his pretensions to the French throne when he signed the Treaty of Calais despite his victories over John II and Philip VI. The father of Edward the Black Prince and John of Gaunt, name this victor at the Battle of Crecy, the English king who started the Hundred Years' War.

A diversion at Wavre meant that a third of the losing army missed out on this battle, in which a preliminary attack on the cheateau Hougoumont also turned out to be a waste of time. When one marshal took the La Haye Sainte farmhouse in the evening, his reinforcements only showed up an hour later, by which time H.E.K. Zieten's corps had arrived to drive him out. Karl von Bulow's attack on the Eastern flank occupied much of the French firepower at this battle, which saw the death of Thomas Picton. Following a bungled French victory at Quatre-Bras and an actual French victory at Ligny, Lord Uxbridge led the Charge of the Scots Greys at this battle. Name this battle fought south of Brussels near the end of the Hundred Days period, a victory for Field Marshal Blucher and the Duke of Wellington and the final defeat of Napoleon.

This text attacks unfunded debt by arguing that government "foresees the facility of borrowing, and therefore dispenses itself from the duty of saving." It also explains how hoarding is a behavior that can only come from mistrust of government, and that it is an opulent populace that allows governments the luxury of carrying debts. One part of this book analyzes the state of agriculture and the shift in power between the countryside and the cities following the fall of the Roman Empire. The example of making a pin is used to illustrate the value of the division of labor in its first section, while a later part looks at the reasons for establishing colonies and the benefits that they provide to question the economic system of mercantilism. Also known for its discussion of the "invisible hand," name this book by Adam Smith.

The third most popular party in this election had no official candidate and was known as the Texas Regulars. Leading candidates for the losing party in this election included Harold Stassen and Robert Taft, who, in a surprise move, instead supported John Bricker; that party's eventual candidate all but locked up his nomination after receiving 14 of the 21 delegates from the Wisconsin primary. The incumbent in this election chose a new vice- presidential candidate because of his former vice-president's association with the Russian spiritualist Nicholas Roerich- that substitution consisted of replacing Henry Wallace with a Missouri senator, Harry Truman. Name this election in which Thomas Dewey lost to Franklin Delano Roosevelt, who won a fourth term.

J.D. Bekenstein wrote a paper in which he generalized this law to black hole formation. This law can be stated mathematically as the indefinite integral of 1 over T dee-Q is greater than zero, and the fluctuation theorem is sometimes used to resolve a paradox concerning a flaw in Boltzmann's H-Theorem regarding this law; that statement is named for Loschmidt. Rudolf Clausius was the first formulator of this law, stating that heat cannot flow spontaneously from a hotter to a cooler object. When considered in terms of heat engines, this law also states that it is impossible to extract heat of a reservoir and have all of it perform work. An imaginary creature sorting particles based on speed, Maxwell's Demon, was unable to violate this law. FTP, name this law of thermodynamics which states that an isolated system will see an increase in entropy.

One story holds that this ruler was asked to turn a housewife's cakes, but let his focus drift to his people's suffering, and angered the housewife by allowing her cakes to burn. Impressed by the wit of a swineherd named Denewulf, this man made Denewulf Bishop of Winchester. This ruler split up the kingdom of Ceolwulf II of Merica, and he was succeeded by his daughter Aethelflaed. After waiting for months in the swamps of Athelney, this ruler won a victory over King Guthrum, whom he converted to Christianity with the Peace of Wedmore. Also known for translating Beothius's Consolation of Philosophy into his native tongue, name this Anglo-Saxon king who, at the battle of Edington, fended the Danes away from Wessex.

This ruler experimented with his country's constitution by drafting the "October Diploma" and the "February Patent," and one incident from the later part of his reign was his veto of the appointment of Cardinal Mariano Rampolla to the Papacy. His marriage to a woman known as Sisi produced only one heir, Rudolf, who was discovered dead along with his lover Mary Vetsera in the Mayerling Incident. Succeeded by Charles I, this ruler took the throne after the abdication of his mentally-deficient uncle, Ferdinand I. This man gave up Venetia in Peace of Prague after his forces were defeated at Koniggratz during a war with Prussia. Name this Austro-Hungarian emperor whose long reign lasted from 1848-1916 and whose nephew was Franz Ferdinand.

One commander who served under this dyansty, Qi Jiguang, fought off pirates at battles fought in Zhejiang and Nan'ao. One emperor of this dynasty was held hostage by Esen Khan after a disastrous attack against the Mongols, but later returned to the throne as Emperor Tianshun. Emperors of this dynasty were guarded by a secret police called the Jinyi Wei. The final emperor of this dynasty hung himself on Coal Hill after the capital was captured by the emperor of the Shun Dynasty, the ‘Dashing Hero' Li Zicheng. This dynasty was founded after the Red Turban Rebellion by a peasant named Zhu Yuanzhang who took a name meaning "vast military," the Hongwu Emperor. This dynasty also patronized the voyages of Zheng He. Name this Chinese dynasty that preceded the Qing and had lots of pottery.

This ruler faced the August Coup, led by a group that formed the State Emergency Committee; that uprising led to the arrest of the Gang of Eight. One of his first actions was to institute a tax on liquor that caused a disastrous reduction in government revenues because of an increased black market for alcohol. Another of his early moves was replacing long-time foreign minister Andrei Gromyko with Eduard Shevardnadze. One of his policies, gospriyomka, referred to stricter state supervision of quality control in manufacturing, while the Law of Cooperatives was included in his policy of openness, which he termed Glasnost. Also known for enacting restructuring, or perestroika, name this last leader of communist Russia who was succeeded by Boris Yeltzin.

One member of this group wrote Nègres blancs d'Amérique while imprisoned for activites related to this group. While plans by members of this group to kidnap Israeli and United States consuls failed, they did detonate bombs in mailboxes and factories, and at Mayor Jean Drapeau's home. This group's actions would lead to the rise of a political party whose supporters called themselves péquistes and a referendum on sovereignty-association. Members of this group kidnapped British Trade Commissioner James Cross and Minister of Labour and Immigration Pierre Laporte. In response, Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau invoked the War Measures Act; Laporte's kidnappers killed him a day later. Name this separatist group associated with the October Crisis in Québec.

This man argued that the U.S. Invasion of Iraq serves as a warning to Iran and North Korea that they can dissuade U.S. Military action by having proper defenses in his article "Dilemmas of Dominance," while analyzed the roots for Middle Eastern contempt of the U.S. Going back to the policies of the Eisenhower administration is his article "9/11: Lessons Unlearned;" both of those pieces were included in his book Interventions. He claimed that American intellectuals could be held responsible for the events of the Vietnam War in his book American Power and the New Mandarins. At the highest level of his namesake hierarchy, a Turing Machine can regonize all languages that are generated. Name this proposer of X-bar theory and developer of generative grammar, the author of Syntactic Structures and a noted anarchist and professor of linguistics at MIT.

The French forces at this battle, since they were waiting for some 5,000 troops under the command of the Dukes of Brabant, Anjou, and Brittany, delayed their attack for over three hours after sunrise, but were prompted by an unexpected enemy advance. One French success was their attack on the enemy's supplies under the command of a native named Yzembart. Their commander, Charles d'Albret, split his troops into three lines and personally commanded their vanguard, though the narrowness of the battlefield spelled their defeat because it meant that they were vulnerable to Thomas Epringham's archers as they marched across a muddy field in full armor, some of them on horseback. Name this English victory of Henry V during the Hundred Years' War.

One force of these peoples, led in part by Cerethrius and Bolgios, defeated a force of Greeks under Calippus at a battle fought at Thermopylae. They were defeated in the Battle of Bibracte before winning a decisive victory at Atuatuca Tungrorum under the command of Ambiorix; those events happened in their namesake war, which also saw battles at Gergovia and Alesia that involved Vercingetorix and Julius Caesar, who wrote a commentary about that conflict. This man's Scottish campaign saw George Monck sack Dundee as well as a decisive victory despite being besieged by David Leslie in the Battle of Dunbar. While allied with the French, his armies won victories at Magenta and Solferino. During his reign, The March of The Thousand by Garibaldi led to the annexation of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. One notable case on this concept involved D.C.'s red light cameras. The "offensive" form of this concept was frowned upon in Parklane Hosiery Co. V. In 1850, the Supreme Court of Massachusetts accepted this standard in a case stemming from a man who was trying to beat two dogs with a cudgel, Brown v. Kendall. The New Jersey Supreme Court applied the "fair share" doctrine to this practice in Southern Burlington County NAACP v. Mt. Laurel. Maldonato, the court stated that the defendant committed an offense arising from this action in its joint form alongside a federal agent who had placed a suitcase inside of a closet. Justice Stewart incredulously compared the crime at the center of this case to the "crime of the common cold." This case's majority opinion cited with approval Pufendorf's apprehension over the significance of a mortal wound. The plaintiff in this case had the amusing first name of Lodowick.
